summary: Mark Juergensmeyer is a scholar of religious studies and Indology. He studied at the University of Illinois, Union Theological Seminary, Columbia University, and UC Berkeley. He held professorships at Claremont McKenna College and UC Santa Barbara.

Mark L. Blum works in Buddhist studies and Japanology. He held posts at the University at Albany, SUNY, and is attested as Professor and Shinjo Ito Distinguished Chair in Japanese Studies at UC Berkeley and the Numata Center.

Mark McClish specializes in Indology and religious studies. He completed doctoral studies under Patrick Olivelle and held positions at Birmingham-Southern College and with Anthem South Asian Normative Traditions Studies.
Mark Owen is a scholar of religious studies and Buddhist studies. He completed his doctoral studies under the supervision of Anna King and Elizabeth Stuart.
Mark Pedersen specializes in computational linguistics. He completed his PhD at the University of Queensland by 2001 and subsequently held a post there.
Mark Rowe is a scholar in religious studies, Japanology, and Buddhist studies. He has served as an Associate Professor of Religious Studies at McMaster University.

Mark S. G. Dyczkowski was an Indologist who studied at Banaras Hindu University, the University of Oxford under Richard Gombrich and Alexis Sanderson, and Sampurnanand Sanskrit University, alongside studying under several traditional teachers.

Mark Siderits is a scholar of philosophy, Buddhist studies, and Indology. He served as an Emeritus Professor of Philosophy at Illinois State University (~1979–2008) and Seoul National University (~2008–2012).

Mark Singleton is an Indology and religious studies scholar. He studied under Elizabeth De Michelis, earned a PhD at the University of Cambridge, and served as a Senior Research Fellow at SOAS University of London.

Mark T. Unno is a scholar of Buddhist studies, religious studies, and Japanology. He studied at Oberlin College and Stanford University, and held positions at Brown University and the University of Oregon.

Mark Tatz was a scholar of Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and Indology. He earned his PhD at the University of British Columbia under Leon Hurvitz, studied under traditional teachers, and was a professor at the California Institute of Integral Studies.

Mark Teeuwen is a Japanology and religious studies scholar. He completed his MA and PhD at Leiden University. He was a lecturer at Cardiff University (1994–1999) and became a professor at the University of Oslo in 1999.
Mark Wilks was a scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as Resident at the Kingdom of Mysore (~1803–1808) and as Governor of the Government of Saint Helena (~1813–1816).
Markus Gabriel is a philosopher who studied at the University of Bonn. He held positions at Bonn, UC Berkeley, The New School, and the Kyoto Institute of Philosophy.

Markus Viehbeck specializes in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He completed his PhD at the University of Vienna under Helmut Tauscher and Franz-Karl Ehrhard, and held positions at Heidelberg University and the University of Vienna.

Marsha Weidner is a scholar of Sinology, history, archaeology, and Buddhist studies. She earned her PhD at UC Berkeley and held art history faculty positions at the University of Virginia and the University of Kansas.

Marshall Sahlins was a scholar of history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Michigan and Columbia University, and served on the faculties of the University of Michigan (~1957–1973) and the University of Chicago (from 1973).

Marta Sernesi is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. She completed her PhD at the University of Turin in 2007 and has served as a Gastprofessorin at the Göttingen Academy of Sciences and Humanities.

Martha Ann Selby is an Indologist. She is a professor emeritus at the University of Texas at Austin and serves as the Sangam Professor of South Asian Studies and Department Chair at Harvard University.

Martha Nussbaum is a philosopher who studied at Wellesley, NYU, Harvard, and under Bernard Williams. She held posts at Harvard, Oxford, and Brown, before becoming Ernst Freund Distinguished Service Professor at the University of Chicago in 1995.
